newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-AWB no sleeping giant as it faces future.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-AWB no sleeping giant as it faces future.

text.p: The outgoing managing director of the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) rankles at the suggestion that the organisation, which turned over A$4.5 billion in its latest year and stands on the doorstep of privatisation, is a waking giant.
"It's never been ... sleeping. It's always been a highly successful grain marketer and trader," John Lawrenson, AWB managing director for seven years, said in a recent interview.

Perhaps it is just that the AWB is more visible in the wider business community today as it prepares for its biggest tests, privatisation and a competition policy review, as well as a possible A$700 million-A$800 million share market float.

The group, still celebrating the successful marketing of a record 23 million tonne crop, has just been given a government go-ahead for a grower-owned structure which will take it through the 1999 end of Federal government guarantees on its A$3 billion a year borrowing programme.
It is also preparing for a government competition review which will decide whether it keeps its export monopoly.
While all this requires a more prominent public profile than the AWB has had before, Lawrenson prefers to describe the organisation as embarking on a next logical development stage.
Australia's Minister for Primary Industries John Anderson announced last Thursday that the statutory authority would become a private grower-owned company.
The privatised AWB's export monopoly of Australian wheat is to be "enshrined" in legislation. But the so-called "single desk" will still have to pass a competition review in 1999/2000.
The restructure would provide the AWB with greater commercial flexibility, "a very welcome move", Lawrenson said.
"After June 30 1999 the only involvement by government will be the granting of the single desk," he said.
Lawrenson is "very confident" the AWB will be permitted to retain its monopoly export power, which has been widely seen as one of the organisation's marketing strengths.
The review will require the monopoly to demonstrate a net benefit to Australia. "I think we continue to (see) the benefit of the single desk (in) additional returns," Lawrenson said.
Recent reviews of rice marketing in New South Wales and sugar marketing in Queensland had recommended that monopoly export marketing arrangements continue, he noted.
"If there is a benefit it should continue. I'm quite sure that as in the past we'll ... demonstrate the benefit," he said.
The new structure for the AWB would allow it to capture even greater benefits from market surges before the review, he said.

Benefits, seen as beginning to fully flow in 1999 when the new company became fully farmer-owned, would be through greater commercial flexibility, an adequate capital base and a shareholder-elected board of directors, Lawrenson said.
Lawrenson pointed to several major achievements achieved during his time with the AWB.
Since domestic grains market de-regulation in 1990, a very competitive trading structure had been set up within the AWB, with capital at risk. "That's been a great success."

Product branding and differentiation had produced some very good premiums out of the export market through the matching of product with customer needs. "I think we can do that better than any other exporting country, by a long way," he said.
The transition to a much more commercial internal structure was important, as was investment downstream, he said.

The AWB was investing in flour milling activities in China and Egypt, was about to fund one mill in Vietnam and had announced last week it would enter a joint-venture with the Japanese agricultural group Zennoh to market feedgrains into Japan, he said.
"Over time that will bring enormous benefits," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
